Backtesting isn't about proving that your strategy works.

It's about discovering how the strategy behaves.

How often does it lose?
How long can losing streaks last?
Where do most profits come from?
Which market environments hurt it?
How sensitive is it to execution costs?

An average return tells you surprisingly little about what you'll actually have to endure to earn it.

Study the journey of the equity curve, not just the destination of the final data.

Micropayments get easier when AI agents can spend without asking

ARK Invest's Brett Winton on why AI agents will almost inevitably need digital assets

"Previously, the difference between free and 5 cents was like an infinite difference in terms of your ability to actually get somebody to do something, because the cognitive burden of spending 5 cents is too high for the end user."

"But if the agent is sitting there with a balance of money that it can spend as it sees fit to provide you with what you need, that could be data, an incremental service."

text:
That tracks with my experience. I've written 4 non-fiction books with my wife (who graduated summa cum laude with a degree in journalism) acting as primary editor.

The first thing she ever edited for me was a piece that Barron's published in 1992. I—having been the Editor-in-Chief of my High School newspaper and a long-time writer—thought the version I gave to her only needed a bit of polishing. 

What came back from her was a SEA of red ink with innumerable corrections and rewrites. 

I was livid! Not only was my ego crushed, I turned it into a huge fight with her, accusing her of trying to drain all of my wonderfully creative darlings out of the piece and replacing them with pedestrian prose for the sake of clarity. The fight got so heated we ended up not speaking about it for the rest of the day.

But then I dutifully went through my original draft and made all of the changes she recommended and the scales fell from eyes—her edited version of my original draft was VASTLY better than my draft. I immediately confessed this to her while simultaneously begging her to be the primary editor on the first book I wrote called "Invest Like the Best."

In hindsight, this was the best thing that could have ever happened to my writing career. Yes, I was emotionally wounded by the harsh criticism, but it was clearly needed. I'm of the opinion that ALL writers, no matter how gifted, could see their work materially improved by a gifted, honest to the point of inflicting emotional damage

For example $AMD trades at ~47x forward earnings but earnings are expected to grow from $5.71 in 2026 to $20.29 in 2028 implying a ~89% earnings CAGR and PEG of ~0.5x.

- $SIVE is targeting T1 hyperscaler deployments for pluggables, CPO, NPO. Not quite sure what you mean by Tier 2. 

They have direct engagements with hyperscalers but currently are more upstream by qualifying with companies like Ayar, $JBL, $GFS, O-Net that eventually likely ends up -> $AMZN / $MSFT for example. 

On financing: 

- Colo players like $CIFR still need $1B+ of financing for their sites.
- Neoclouds like $CRWV need billions of financing to buy GPUs.

Higher rates + less support for financing makes it more challenging for these players. 

$SIVE already raised 700M SEK for their buildout and largely rely on external foundries, so they don't have financing constraints. 

There's pressure on players that need currently need financing for capex, but markets group up everyone in AI sector indiscriminately. 

The second nuance is whether or not this effects the end customers in terms of demand. 

I'd argue optical sector is insulated, even if overall AI capex from hyperscalers decreases, I see optical content still rising and aggregate demand rising. 

And this is especially the case with new incoming players going through their first qual cycles.
